course: CSEG3060 — Research Methodology in Computer Science
assessment: Quiz 1 (Set A) — Unit I · CCVT batches
instructions: 25 questions · 30 minutes · 25 marks (1 per question). This quiz does not test definitions — every question gives you a situation and asks you to diagnose it, exactly as the in-class drills did. Read each scenario fully before answering; the distractors are all things students actually say. Questions marked 'select all that apply' are graded on the exact set — a partial selection scores zero, so choose deliberately. There is no negative marking. Your score is not shown at the end; results are released after the quiz.

questions.topic: I.1 — Task vs project vs research problem
questions.question: A student proposes: “I will build a face-recognition attendance system and deploy it in our department.” Which single change would convert this from a project into a research problem?

options.A: Use a deeper CNN architecture than the one in the tutorial
options.B: Add a named baseline and a metric, and ask whether the system beats it under stated conditions
options.C: Increase the training set from 2,000 to 10,000 face images
options.D: Write the final report in IEEE two-column format

questions.explanation: Task, project and research problem differ on one axis only: is the outcome already known? Building a face-recognition system has a known outcome — it is a project. It becomes research when a defensible claim is attached: versus what baseline, on which metric, under which conditions. Depth of model, dataset size and report formatting change none of that.

questions.question: Three of these could be research problems. Which one cannot, because no possible experimental result would make its author say “I was wrong”?

options.A: Attention pruning degrades accuracy more on code-mixed Hinglish than on English
options.B: Our framework leverages cutting-edge AI to deliver a next-generation learning experience
options.C: Test selection can cut CI time by more than 40% without missing regressions
options.D: Using an AI coding assistant changes defect density in first-year students' code

questions.explanation: A research problem must be refutable. A, C and D each name something that could come out the other way. B names no construct, no metric and no comparison, so no result could contradict it — which also means no result could support it.

questions.question: Which of these is the clearest example of basic rather than applied research?

options.A: Tuning a bank's fraud model to its own transaction volume
options.B: Deriving the information-theoretic limit on how far a class of sources can be compressed
options.C: Migrating a hospital records system from on-premise servers to the cloud
options.D: A/B testing two checkout button placements on a shopping site

questions.explanation: Basic research seeks knowledge that holds regardless of a particular deployment. A derived limit constrains every future scheme for that source class. A, C and D are all valuable, but each is tied to one organisation's immediate goal.

questions.question: In 2006 everyone in computer vision was tuning models on datasets of tens of thousands of images. Fei-Fei Li read the same literature and asked whether the bottleneck was the data rather than the model — which led to ImageNet. Which source of research problems does this illustrate?

options.A: An explicit gap stated in a paper's Future Work section
options.B: A population gap — a method untested on a new group
options.C: A contradiction between two published papers
options.D: An assumption everybody shared and nobody had tested

questions.explanation: The assumption gap is the hardest to see and the highest in payoff: nothing in the literature says 'the data might be the bottleneck', because everyone had silently agreed it was not. Explicit Future Work gaps are the most crowded; assumption gaps are where the field turns.

questions.question: A student says: “Our CI pipeline is so slow, it drives the whole team mad.” What is the correct FIRST step in converting this irritation into a research problem?

options.A: Search Google Scholar for papers on continuous integration
options.B: Measure it — how slow, for which builds, and at what cost per week
options.C: Switch to a faster CI provider and see whether the team is happier
options.D: Write the problem statement immediately, while the irritation is fresh

questions.explanation: An irritation you cannot measure stays an opinion. The conversion chain is: irritation → measure it → is it general? → has it been solved? → problem statement. Searching and writing both come after there is a number.

questions.question: A student replicates a 2019 published claim on 2026 data, following the original protocol carefully. The result reproduces almost exactly. What should they do?

options.A: Nothing — a replication that succeeds is not a result
options.B: Vary the dataset until some difference appears, so there is something to report
options.C: Report it, explicitly including the fact that it reproduced
options.D: Reframe the work as a novel method to make it publishable

questions.explanation: Replication is a legitimate source of research problems precisely because either outcome is a result — provided you report honestly, including when it does reproduce. Option B is metric shopping; option D is dishonest framing.

questions.question: Apply the calibration rule to this sentence: “Deep learning for medical imaging in India.” Roughly how many distinct final-year projects would satisfy it, and what does that tell you?

options.A: About 1 — this is a research question, ready to work on
options.B: Between 5 and 20 — this is a topic, not yet a question
options.C: More than 100 — this is a field, not a question
options.D: Zero — it has been over-narrowed and nobody would care

questions.explanation: The rule: ask how many distinct final-year projects would satisfy the sentence. Over 100 means a field; 5–20 a topic; about 1 means you finally have a question; 0 means you narrowed past the point where anyone cares.

questions.question: You are narrowing “hate-speech detection” using the five knobs — population, task, comparison, metric and setting. Which strategy produces a workable research question?

options.A: Turn one knob, choosing a metric and leaving the rest open
options.B: Turn about three knobs, for example population, comparison and setting
options.C: Turn all five knobs as tightly as they will go
options.D: Leave the knobs alone and add more datasets instead

questions.explanation: Turn one and you are still describing a field. Turn all five and you have engineered away everything interesting — nobody cares about the answer. About three is the working range.

questions.question: Your experimental plan compares 2 methods on 3 datasets, with 3 seeds each and 1 ablation. Your supervisor says: “Also compare against one more baseline — it's just one more method.” Using runs = methods × datasets × seeds × (1 + ablations), how many EXTRA runs does that one baseline cost?

options.A: 1 extra run
options.B: 3 extra runs
options.C: 9 extra runs
options.D: 18 extra runs

questions.explanation: One extra method multiplies through everything else: 3 datasets × 3 seeds × (1 + 1 ablation) = 18 runs. Scope creep is multiplicative, not additive, which is why 'just one more baseline' is never a small request.

questions.question: A problem scores Feasible 5, Interesting 5, Novel 5, Ethical 1, Relevant 5, Measurable 5. What is the correct verdict?

options.A: Average is 4.3 out of 5 — comfortably above threshold, proceed
options.B: Very strong problem; the ethics issue can be sorted out later in the semester
options.C: Fatal — the criteria multiply, so a single 1 kills the problem regardless of the rest
options.D: Acceptable provided the supervisor signs an approval form

questions.explanation: FINER + M is a product, not an average. Any single 1 makes the product zero. A 5-5-5-5-5-1 problem is a dead problem — and a hard ethics failure has exactly one repair move: abandon.

questions.question: AlphaGo would score 5 for Feasibility at DeepMind and 1 for a final-year team. What does this demonstrate about the F criterion?

options.A: That feasibility is really a measure of novelty in disguise
options.B: That feasibility is relative to your own data, compute, time, skill and access
options.C: That feasibility only matters for industry projects, not academic ones
options.D: That feasibility can be ignored if the problem is sufficiently relevant

questions.explanation: Feasibility is never a property of the problem alone. Five resources multiply — data, compute, time, skill, access — and each is measured against what you personally can obtain this semester.

questions.question: A team operationalises “code quality” as the number of comment lines per KLOC. Which problem does this metric have?

options.A: Only a validity gap — the metric has drifted from the construct
options.B: Only a gaming gap — the metric can be won without the construct
options.C: Both: it no longer means code quality, and it can be maximised by typing comments
options.D: Neither — the construct has been operationalised, which is what was required

questions.explanation: Both gaps are open. The validity gap: comment density is not what anyone means by code quality. The gaming gap: a developer can raise it in an afternoon without improving a single line of logic. A better operationalisation is defects surviving review per KLOC.

questions.question: A well-stated, novel, ethical problem requires three years of hospital records, behind an approval process the team has not yet applied for and which typically takes eight months. Which repair move actually fixes this?

options.A: Narrow the scope to fewer patients and a shorter time window
options.B: Re-anchor to a public, de-identified corpus and state the limitation honestly
options.C: Re-measure using a different accuracy metric on the same records
options.D: Proceed as planned and record the delay as a limitation in the final report

questions.explanation: Narrowing fixes scope, never access — a smaller slice of inaccessible data is still inaccessible. Only re-anchoring to data you can actually obtain repairs a resource-blind problem, and only re-anchoring saves the semester.

questions.question: A student argues: “I searched thoroughly and found no recent papers on this, so it must be an open problem.” What is wrong with that inference?

options.A: Nothing — an absence of recent literature is the standard test for an open problem
options.B: Absence of papers usually means the question is closed, not open
options.C: It means the topic is too narrow to interest a research community
options.D: It means the search terms were in English rather than the local language

questions.explanation: A question with no recent literature is in one of three states: solved and moved into textbooks, of interest to nobody, or genuinely open — and the third is rarest. Distinguish them by reading surveys and textbooks, not by counting recent papers.

questions.question: Which rewrite genuinely repairs “We will improve the user experience of the college ERP using modern web technologies”?

options.A: We will rebuild the ERP front-end in React with a responsive Tailwind design
options.B: We will significantly enhance the usability and overall performance of the ERP
options.C: Across three core ERP tasks, does a redesigned navigation raise unaided task-completion by at least 15 percentage points and cut median time-on-task below 90 seconds, for n = 30 second-year students?
options.D: We will conduct a survey asking students how satisfied they are with the ERP

questions.explanation: The error is unfalsifiability, so the repair is re-measure: construct → operational definition → metric → threshold. Only C names the tasks, the metrics, the thresholds and the population. A is method-first, B renames the vagueness, D measures opinion rather than the construct.

questions.question: When a FINER + M criterion fails, exactly four moves are available. Which of these is NOT one of them?

options.A: Narrow — shrink the scope until feasibility is true
options.B: Re-measure — replace the metric while keeping the question
options.C: Abandon — stop, and save the semester
options.D: Keep the problem and hope the criterion stops mattering by the review

questions.explanation: Narrow, re-anchor, re-measure and abandon are the four moves. Hoping is the popular fifth option and it is not on the list — the criterion does not stop mattering, it simply resurfaces at the review panel, in week twelve instead of week three.

questions.question: A proposal states: “The ethics approval permits only 30 participants.” In the scope section of a research report, this sentence belongs under:

options.A: Scope — it defines what the study includes
options.B: Delimitations — it is a boundary the researcher has chosen
options.C: Limitations — it is a constraint imposed on the researcher
options.D: Objectives — it defines what the study will achieve

questions.explanation: Scope is what you include, by choice. Delimitations are what you exclude, by choice, with a reason. Limitations are imposed on you — you did not pick the number 30, a committee did. Declared, a limitation protects the claim; hidden, it destroys it at the viva.

questions.topic: I.6 — Objectives that can be checked
questions.question: Four specific objectives are proposed. Which one would be marked down immediately?

options.A: Quantify the top-1 accuracy drop from lab to field images across three crops (Table 3)
options.B: Understand how transformer models behave when the input data is noisy
options.C: Compare three published models on a single held-out test set (Table 1)
options.D: Measure p95 inference latency on a sub-$80 handset over 100 runs (Figure 2)

questions.explanation: “Understand” names a state of mind: it produces no artefact, so neither you nor an examiner can ever check whether it was achieved. Objectives use measurable verbs — measure, compare, quantify, characterise, evaluate, attribute — and each maps to one experiment and one table or figure.

questions.question: Which of these hypotheses takes the biggest risk, and is therefore the strongest?

options.A: Accuracy will differ between lab images and field images
options.B: Field accuracy will be lower than lab accuracy
options.C: Field top-1 accuracy will be at least 15 points lower, and illumination normalisation will recover at least half of that gap
options.D: Our model will perform well under real field conditions

questions.explanation: C can fail in three distinct ways — the drop is under 15 points, normalisation recovers less than half, or it makes things worse — and it states its own refutation condition in advance. A is non-directional, B is directional but cheap, D is unfalsifiable.

questions.topic: I.6 — The chain from problem to claim
questions.question: A study's research question asks WHY field accuracy drops. Its objectives only quantify HOW MUCH it drops. Its conclusion states that the drop is “caused by poor illumination”. At which join does the chain first break?

options.A: Problem → Question
options.B: Question → Objectives
options.C: Method → Data
options.D: Metric → Claim

questions.explanation: The break happens as soon as an explanatory question is handed to objectives that only measure magnitude. Nothing downstream can repair it: with no ablation or controlled intervention, the causal sentence in the conclusion is unsupported however good the experiments are.

questions.question: A claim states: “No deterministic protocol can solve consensus in an asynchronous system if even one process may crash.” Which investigative approach could settle it?

options.A: Experimental — implement many protocols and measure how they behave
options.B: Simulation — model the network at large scale and observe failures
options.C: Analytical — construct a proof, because the claim quantifies over all possible protocols
options.D: Design science — build a protocol and evaluate whether it succeeds

questions.explanation: An impossibility claim ranges over every protocol that could ever be written. No experiment or simulation can range over all of them — testing is sampling. Only a proof settles a universal claim, which is exactly the Pentium FDIV lesson.

questions.question: A team simulates a gossip protocol at one million nodes and reports that it converges within 10 rounds. What must the study include before that number counts as evidence?

options.A: More random seeds and a longer simulated run time
options.B: Validation of the simulator against a small real deployment, plus stated fidelity limits
options.C: A larger cloud budget so the simulation can be repeated more often
options.D: A user study confirming that operators trust the protocol

questions.explanation: A simulation inherits its validity from the simulator. Without validating against a real trace you have measured a program you wrote, not a protocol. Validation and a sensitivity sweep are part of the work, not optional extras.

questions.question: A paper reports: “We tuned our method over 200 trials. The baseline was run with its published default settings.” Which validity is threatened?

options.A: Internal — two things differ between the arms, so the effect cannot be attributed to the method
options.B: External — the result may not hold outside the sample studied
options.C: Construct — the metric may not measure the named concept
options.D: Conclusion — the statistics may not support a claim of that strength

questions.explanation: The method AND the tuning effort both differ, so any difference in results could be caused by either. What was measured is the team's effort, not the method. The fix is equal tuning budgets, reported explicitly.

questions.question: In a medical imaging study each patient contributed about 40 images, and the images were split randomly into training and test sets. What is the defect, and why does it matter?

options.A: Class imbalance — one condition dominates the dataset
options.B: Temporal leakage — the model trains on the future and predicts the past
options.C: Group leakage — the same patient appears on both sides, so the model can recognise the patient rather than the disease
options.D: No defect — random splitting is the standard, unbiased procedure

questions.explanation: The split must be by the group that shares information — patient, user, repository, document — not by the individual record. Group leakage is silent and always flattering: accuracy rises, no error appears, and the defect only surfaces on genuinely new patients.

questions.question: A student reports 97% accuracy on a dataset in which 97% of records belong to a single class, and writes that the model “performs excellently”. What must be reported before that sentence means anything?

options.A: The total training time and the number of model parameters
options.B: The do-nothing majority-class baseline, which also scores about 97%
options.C: The learning rate and optimiser used during training
options.D: The number of epochs before the validation loss stopped falling

questions.explanation: With a 97/3 split, always predicting the majority class scores 97% — so the reported number demonstrates nothing at all. Class balance is part of the ten-minute descriptive audit you do before modelling, and the trivial baseline belongs in the results table.
